title: Recursion: Fibonacci
oneLiner: Factorial calls itself once per call. This calls itself TWICE -- and that branching is where recursion's cost can quietly explode.
keyTakeaway: fib(n) = fib(n-1) + fib(n-2) branches into two recursive calls at every step (unlike Factorial's one), and those two calls share massive overlap -- fib(n-1) and fib(n-2) both end up separately recomputing fib(n-3), fib(n-4), and so on, all the way down. The call count roughly doubles per level, giving O(2^n) -- the exact kind of explosion Big O's chart shows pulling away from everything else. Remembering (memoizing) results already computed is the fix, and it's the entire idea behind Dynamic Programming.
explanation: The Fibonacci sequence is defined recursively: fib(0) = 0, fib(1) = 1, and every fib(n) after that is fib(n-1) + fib(n-2) -- each term is the sum of the two before it (0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, ...). Written exactly as defined, the recursive implementation calls itself TWICE per call instead of Factorial's once, which changes the shape entirely: the call tree branches, and the SAME smaller sub-calls (fib(2), fib(3), ...) get recomputed from scratch by many different branches independently, with zero memory that they were already solved. Step through the visualization and watch how many times small values like fib(1) get computed completely separately -- that repeated, wasted work is exactly what memoization (caching each fib(n) the first time it's computed, then returning the cached value instead of recursing again) eliminates, which is a later lesson's whole point. Watch out for the TWO base cases -- fib(0) = 0 AND fib(1) = 1 both need to stop the recursion, not just one of them.

visualizationSteps.message: fib(4) -- not a base case. Call fib(3) first, then fib(2).
fib(3) -- not a base case. Call fib(2) first, then fib(1).
fib(2) -- not a base case. Call fib(1) first, then fib(0).
fib(2) -- not a base case. Call fib(1) first, then fib(0).

complexity.note: Each call spawns two more, so the call tree roughly doubles per level (exponential time); but only one root-to-leaf path is on the stack at once, so space is just the depth, O(n).
